name: Rosa Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Dr Costa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Rosa, please. I work at the Church Street clinic in the hill town where I grew up, with Dr Benedetti, who delivered half the town and is sixty-six now, and one other doctor. I start at eight, see about twenty-five patients, and in the afternoons I visit the old people who can't come down the hill. Half my patients knew me when I was a girl, which is lovely and also means they tell my mother everything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know the families. When Mrs Russo comes in, I know her husband died in March and I know she's not really here about her knee. What wears me out is the computer, the forms, and the endless messages from the health authority in the city about new systems. I've never used AI and I don't want to. Money is tight because my husband Matteo is a carpenter and work is slow in winter, and we spent everything on the wedding last year, so we've got maybe three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Good. That's what I've thought all along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: I told you so. At church on Sunday, at my parents' table, I'd say the people in the city got excited about a toy. A doctor's job is people, and people don't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, but it doesn't fix the things I really worry about. Matteo's winter work, the three weeks of savings, and Dr Benedetti retiring in a year or two, which might mean the clinic gets merged with the one down in the valley. There aren't other clinics up here, and I don't want to leave the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, and keep learning from Dr Benedetti while he's still here. Matteo and I would put £100 a month aside, starting in January, because we want a baby in the next couple of years. And I'd go to the health authority meeting about the clinic's future, which I'd normally skip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly at peace. A little worry about the clinic and about money, but that's life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the clinic merges with the one in the valley?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd drive forty minutes each way, and the old people up here would have to come down the hill, which many of them can't. I'd fight that, quietly. I'd talk to the mayor, who was in my brother's class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a doctor's job is people. Is there anything about the paperwork that you'd be glad to see automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the forms for the city. But honestly, I'd rather do them myself than trust a machine to fill them in wrong. If something goes wrong with a patient, it's my name on the notes, not the computer's.

say: I'd say **I told you so**: the city got excited about a toy.
A doctor's job is **people**, and people don't change.
think: It's a **relief**, but my real worries are still there.
Matteo's **winter work**, three weeks of savings and a possible clinic **merger** worry me.
do: Keep learning from **Dr Benedetti** while he's still here.
Save **£100 a month** from January for a baby in the next two years.
Go to the health authority meeting about the **clinic's future**.
feel: Mostly **at peace**, with a little worry about the clinic and money.
S0.quote: If something goes wrong with a patient, it's my name on the notes, not the computer's.
fieldNote: Her worries are **local and old**: savings, Matteo's slow winters, the clinic merger.
Strong **hometown roots**; she won't move from the hill town.
**Distrust** of AI is about responsibility as much as habit.
Would lean on **local ties**, like the mayor from her brother's class.

steps.text: Keep learning from Dr Benedetti at the Church Street clinic
Save £100 a month from January for a baby
Ask the mayor to help keep the hill clinic open

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds like what the health authority keeps promising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we don't want it here. I'd say it to the health authority, kindly but clearly, and I'd say it at church. The old people up the hill don't want a computer answering the phone when Mrs Russo's chest is bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me more than I'd show. If the city decides the clinic can run with one doctor and a computer when Dr Benedetti retires, it won't be the one who never uses AI that they keep. I'm the junior, I'm slow on the computer, and I can't move away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my visits up the hill, because nobody's replacing those. I'd do whatever training they force on us, but I'd wait and see before using anything more. And Matteo and I would put off the baby for a year until we know what the clinic is doing, which breaks my heart a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. Like the ground is shifting under the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the clinic was cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The health authority in the city, and the companies that sell them these systems. The health authority in the city looks at a spreadsheet, not at my patients. Nobody from the city has ever been up our hill in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your family be able to help if your job changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, they would. My father has the bakery and my mother would have us to eat every night. I'd hate to need it, though. We were brought up to stand on our own feet.

say: I'd tell the health authority, **kindly but clearly**, that we don't want it here.
Old people up the hill don't want a **computer** answering the phone.
think: If the clinic runs with **one doctor** and a computer, they won't keep me.
I'm the junior, slow on the computer, and I **can't move** away.
do: Keep doing my **visits up the hill**, which nobody is replacing.
Do the **forced training** only, then wait and see.
Put off having a **baby** for a year until the clinic's future is clear.
feel: **Anxious**, like the ground is shifting under the town.
S1.quote: The health authority in the city looks at a spreadsheet, not at my patients. Nobody from the city has ever been up our hill in January.
fieldNote: Fears the clinic shrinks to **one doctor** when Dr Benedetti retires.
Blames **distant officials** and the companies selling to them.
Delaying a **baby** is the real cost she names.
Family would help, but **pride** in standing on her own feet runs deep.

steps.text: Keep doing the home visits to older patients up the hill
Do only the forced AI training and wait
Put off trying for a baby by a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. My God. That's... no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and someone should stop it. I'd say it at church, to the mayor, to anyone. I'd say a country that replaces its doctors with machines has forgotten what people are for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose my job, or most of it. By 2028 the AI does the thinking, and the city would keep Dr Benedetti's replacement, one experienced doctor, to sign off and do the examinations until the robots come in 2031. That's not me. And Matteo's work is already slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd move in with my parents above the bakery to save the rent. I'd ask Dr Benedetti, the first week, whether there's any way to keep me on for home visits, even part-time. Matteo would take every job he could, even the ones he normally turns down. And the baby would wait, which I'd find very hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like being lost in the hills in fog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mrs Russo if she asked whether you'd still be her doctor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'll always be her doctor, even if they don't pay me. And I'd mean it. I'd go up the hill on my day off if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd work for free? With three weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know it doesn't make sense. But you don't leave people. My grandmother nursed half this town during the war with no wages, and nobody here forgot it.

say: I'd say it's **madness** and someone should stop it.
A country that replaces doctors with machines has **forgotten** what people are for.
think: I'd **lose my job**, or most of it, by 2028.
The city would keep **one experienced** doctor until robots in 2031, and Matteo's work is slow.
do: Move in with my parents **above the bakery** to save the rent.
Ask Dr Benedetti in the **first week** about part-time home visits.
Wait on the **baby**, and Matteo takes every job he can.
feel: **Frightened**, like being lost in the hills in fog.
S2.quote: My grandmother nursed half this town during the war with no wages, and nobody here forgot it.
fieldNote: Expects to **lose the post** while Matteo's income is already thin.
Leans fully on **family**: her parents' flat above the bakery.
Would keep seeing patients **unpaid**, a contradiction she admits.
Her anger is moral: a country that **forgets** what people are for.

steps.text: Move into her parents' flat above the bakery
Ask Dr Benedetti about part-time paid home visits
Delay having a baby until the job is settled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for sensible people to slow it down. I'd say it to the health authority and to the mayor. And I'd say the old people up here still need a doctor who comes to the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried. Dr Benedetti will have retired by then, and I might be the only doctor the clinic has, or the clinic might be gone. The thinking part goes in 2031 and the hands-on visits last until about 2034, so the visits are where I'd make myself needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a course in caring for the dying, palliative care, because that's hands-on, done in people's homes. Nobody wants a machine sitting with them while they die at home. I'd keep saving the £100 a month and add a bit more when Matteo's busy in summer. And I'd wait to see what the systems actually do before I touched them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not lost. Like knowing a hard winter is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have the baby in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, in two years or so. I don't want to plan my children around a machine. If God sends us a baby, we'll manage, my parents will help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's quite different from what you said about the two-year picture. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because five years means I'd have time to find my place. Two years means I'd be fighting for my job with a newborn. Here I'd have time.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to **slow it down**.
Old people up the hill still need a doctor who **comes to the door**.
think: The clinic might have only **one doctor** by then, or be gone.
Home visits last until about **2034**, so I'd make myself needed there.
do: Take a course in **palliative care**, caring for the dying at home.
Keep saving **£100 a month**, more in Matteo's busy summers.
**Wait** to see what the systems do before using them.
feel: **Worried, but not lost**, like a hard winter coming.
S3.quote: Nobody wants a machine sitting with them while they die at home.
fieldNote: She finds a **hands-on** niche: palliative care at home.
Would still have a **baby**, relying on faith and family.
Remains **resistant** to AI tools even with five years' warning.
Anxious because the **clinic itself** may be cut.

steps.text: Take a palliative care course for home-based end-of-life care
Save £100 a month, more in Matteo's busy summers
Hold off using AI systems until they prove themselves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make sure the town keeps its doctors. I'd say it in church and at the town meetings. I'd say a good doctor is someone the patients trust, and you can't put that on a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right for most of it. I'd be thirty-seven in 2036, with children, I hope, and I'd be the doctor everyone up here knows. The machines would come for the paperwork first, and the visits would last until about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, do the palliative care course, and have the baby we want. I'd let the younger doctors learn the machines and keep the visits for myself. And I'd go on saving a little each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a bit uneasy about the town, but calmer about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you worried again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The city cutting us before any of this even came. The real danger is the city closing the Church Street clinic to save money, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd look forward to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not doing the city's forms. If a machine filled those in right, I wouldn't complain. But I'd still check them.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to make sure the town **keeps its doctors**.
A good doctor is someone the patients **trust**, and you can't put that on a machine.
think: I'd likely be **all right** for most of the decade.
Paperwork goes first, and **home visits** would last until about 2039.
do: Have the **baby** we want in the next few years.
Do the **palliative care** course and keep the home visits.
feel: **Calmer** about myself, still a bit uneasy about the town.
S4.quote: The real danger is the city closing the Church Street clinic to save money, AI or not.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her expect her own job to **hold**.
Her real fear stays the **clinic closing** for budget reasons.
Would leave AI to **younger doctors** and keep the visits.
Grudgingly admits machines filling in **forms** would be welcome.

steps.text: Try for a baby in the next two years
Keep the home visits and do the palliative course
Leave learning the AI systems to younger doctors

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd lose my job just when we want a family, and the town would lose its doctor. What would help is the health authority promising to keep a doctor in every small town, and paying for home visits properly. I don't want handouts, I want to keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When people are dying, they ask me to pray with them sometimes. I don't think a machine will ever be asked to do that. If it is, something has gone very wrong.

headlineQuote: When people are dying, they ask me to pray with them sometimes. I don't think a machine will ever be asked to do that.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old** junior doctor in the hill town where she grew up.
She is married to Matteo, a **carpenter** with slow winters, and they want a baby soon.
She is **traditional** and devout, never uses AI, and relies on family and the parish.
She blames **city officials** and the companies selling them systems.
She goes from uneasy to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, settling to uneasy with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing her job just as they start a **family**.
whatWouldHelp: A promise to keep a **doctor** in every **small town**.
Proper pay for **home visits**, not handouts.
